DCD: Double channel duplex — a communication system configuration using two separate frequency channels simultaneously for two-way (duplex) communication, allowing both parties to transmit and receive at the same time, commonly used in air-ground communications.
DCKG: Docking — the process of maneuvering an aircraft into its parking position at a gate or stand, often guided by visual docking guidance systems (VDGS).
DCP: Datum crossing point — a designated point at which an aircraft crosses a specified reference line or datum, used in navigation and flight procedure design.
DCPC: Direct controller-pilot communications — direct voice or data link communication between an air traffic controller and a pilot without relay through another station, ensuring efficient and clear exchange of ATC instructions.
DCS: Double channel simplex — a communication system configuration using two separate frequency channels for two-way communication, but only one direction may transmit at a time (simplex operation on each channel).
DEC: December — the twelfth month of the year, used in aviation date-time groups, NOTAMs, and flight planning documentation.
DEG: Degrees — a unit of measurement for bearing, direction, or angle, used in aviation for navigation, headings, wind direction, and instrument approach procedures.
DEPO: Deposition — the phase change process where water vapor transforms directly into ice without passing through a liquid state; relevant to aircraft icing and weather phenomena.
DER: Departure end of the runway — the far end of the runway opposite the threshold from which an aircraft departs; used as a reference point for departure procedures, obstacle clearance, and takeoff performance calculations.
DES: Descend to or descending to — an instruction or clearance given by ATC for an aircraft to descend to a specified altitude or flight level.
DEST: Destination — the airport or location to which an aircraft is bound, used in flight plans, NOTAMs, and operational communications.
DETRESFA: Distress phase — a phase of emergency declared when an aircraft is in grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance, representing the most serious level of emergency alert.
DEV: Deviation or deviating — a departure from the intended flight path, heading, or clearance; may refer to navigation error, magnetic deviation, or a requested deviation from ATC instructions (e.g., weather deviation).
DF: Direction finding — the process of determining the bearing or direction of a radio signal source using a direction finder (DF) station, used for aircraft navigation and emergency location.
DFDR: Digital flight data recorder — an electronic device that digitally records aircraft flight parameters (altitude, airspeed, heading, attitude, etc.) for accident investigation and safety analysis purposes.
DIF: Diffuse — describing a meteorological condition where sunlight or visibility is scattered and non-directional, often used in reference to diffuse sky radiation or diffuse lighting conditions.
DIST: Distance — the spatial measurement between two points, expressed in nautical miles (NM) in aviation, used for navigation, flight planning, and position reporting.
DIV: Divert or diverting — an operational decision to proceed to an alternate airport or location other than the original destination, typically due to weather, fuel constraints, or emergency situations.
DLY: Daily — occurring or recurring every day; used in NOTAMs and aviation schedules to indicate the daily applicability of a condition, operation, or restriction.
DNG: Danger or dangerous — indicating a hazardous condition, area, or activity that poses a threat to aircraft safety, such as danger areas in airspace or dangerous goods on board.
DOF: Date of flight — the calendar date on which a flight is scheduled or operated, used in flight planning, NOTAMs, and operational coordination.
DOM: Domestic — relating to flight operations, airspace, or regulations within the boundaries of a single country, as distinct from international operations.
DP: Dew point temperature — the temperature to which air must be cooled for water vapor to condense into dew; used in aviation meteorology to assess humidity, fog potential, and icing conditions.
DPT: Depth — the vertical measurement of a substance or feature, such as water depth on a flooded runway or the depth of snow accumulation on movement areas.
DRG: During — a preposition used in NOTAMs and aviation text to specify the time frame or period within which a condition, activity, or restriction applies.
DS: Dust storm — a meteorological phenomenon where strong winds raise large amounts of dust, reducing visibility to less than 1000 meters; reported in METAR and SPECI as 'DS'.
DSB: Double sideband — a type of amplitude modulation (AM) transmission where both the upper and lower sidebands are transmitted, used in some aviation communication and navigation systems.
DTAM: Descend to and maintain — an ATC clearance instructing an aircraft to descend to a specified altitude and then maintain that altitude upon reaching it.
DTG: Date-time group — a standardized alphanumeric representation of date and time (e.g., 251200Z JAN = 25th day, 1200 UTC, January), used in NOTAMs, flight plans, and operational messages.
DTHR: Displaced runway threshold — a runway threshold that is not at the physical beginning of the runway surface; the area before the threshold is available for takeoff and taxi but not for landing.
DTRT: Deteriorate or deteriorating — describing a worsening condition, typically used in weather reports (e.g., deteriorating visibility, ceiling, or braking action).
DTW: Dual tandem wheels — an aircraft landing gear configuration with two sets of tandem wheels on each main gear strut, commonly used on larger transport aircraft to distribute weight.
DU: Dust — fine dry particulate matter suspended in the atmosphere or present on movement areas, which can reduce visibility and affect aircraft operations.
DUC: Dense upper cloud — a thick cloud layer at high altitude that may obscure terrain, reduce visibility, and affect enroute navigation or approach procedures.
DUR: Duration — the length of time during which a condition, event, or activity is expected to continue, used in NOTAMs and flight planning.
DVOR: Doppler VOR — a type of VHF omnidirectional range (VOR) navigation aid that uses Doppler frequency shift principles to reduce site error and provide more accurate bearing information.
DW: Dual wheels — an aircraft landing gear configuration with two wheels mounted side by side on a single strut, providing increased load distribution and redundancy.
DZ: Drizzle — light precipitation consisting of very small water droplets (diameter less than 0.5 mm) that fall close together, reducing visibility; reported in METAR as 'DZ'.
EAT: Expected approach time — the time at which ATC expects an arriving aircraft will be cleared to commence its approach procedure, used for arrival sequencing and holding stack management.
EB: Eastbound — proceeding or directed toward the east; used in flight planning, ATC communications, and route descriptions to indicate direction of travel.
EDA: Elevation differential area — an area on an aerodrome where there is a significant difference in elevation, which may affect aircraft ground movement, visibility, or obstacle clearance assessment.
EET: Estimated elapsed time — the estimated time required to travel from one point to another along a route, used in flight planning and ATC coordination to predict aircraft position.
EFC: Expect further clearance — a phrase used in ATC communications to inform a pilot that additional clearance (e.g., approach clearance) will be issued at a later time, typically while the aircraft is in holding.
ELEV: Elevation — the vertical distance of a point, object, or aerodrome above mean sea level (MSL), expressed in feet or meters, used for obstacle clearance and altimeter settings.
ELR: Extra long range — a classification of aircraft or equipment capable of operating over very long distances without refueling, typically exceeding standard long-range capabilities.
ELT: Emergency locator transmitter — a battery-powered radio transmitter carried on aircraft that automatically activates on impact to broadcast a distress signal on 121.5 MHz and 406 MHz, aiding search and rescue operations.
EM: Emission — the propagation of electromagnetic energy from a transmitter, including radio waves used in aviation communications, navigation, and radar systems.
EMERG: Emergency — a situation involving an immediate or imminent threat to the safety of an aircraft, its occupants, or persons on the ground, requiring urgent action.
ENE: East-northeast — a compass direction midway between east and northeast (67.5 degrees), used in navigation, wind direction reporting, and ATC instructions.
ENG: Engine — a machine that converts fuel into mechanical energy to produce thrust or power for an aircraft, including piston, turboprop, turbofan, turbojet, and turboshaft types.
